newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs honour indicted war criminal.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs honour indicted war criminal.

text.p: Bosnian Serb authorities honoured a notorious police chief as a fallen hero on Sunday, three days after British soldiers shot him dead when he resisted arrest on war crimes charges.
Simo Drljaca, a former police chief of Prijedor who led the ethnic cleansing against Moslems and Croats in 1992, was killed after he opened fire on British troops.

While Bosnian Serbs portrayed his death as murder, British Defence Secretary George Robertson said the attempt to arrest Drljaca signalled a crackdown on suspects wanted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia.
"This (incident) will have upset a lot of people who thought they were getting away with it," he told BBC television.
"What has happened this week is going to make them less easy in their beds and some of them will do rash things, which may well have further consequences."
Drljaca was a powerful ally of the ultra-nationalist leadership and his funeral was treated as an official event by Serb television.
Serb police carried his coffin to a hearse as his family watched. Senior politicians were exected to attend his burial in the northern town of Banja Luka later in the day.
Prosecutors for the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague had charged Drljaca with helping to orchestrate a genocidal campaign between April and December 1992.
His associate, Milan Kovacevic, was seized by British troops, also on Thursday, and extradited to The Hague as part of "Operation Tango".
The NATO raid broke new ground for the alliance which had previously ruled out going after suspects unless peacekeeping troops happened to stumble upon them.
The swoop on war crimes suspects aggravated a power struggle among Bosnian Serbs and the leadership moved to resolve the feud over the weekend.
Seeking to present a united front, Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic met her rival, Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's collective presidency.
The Serbian Orthodox church, which has links to leadership, helped broker the meeting in Banja Luka.

Patriarch Pavle, the highest church authority, travelled to Bosnia's autonomous Serb republic to mediate in the dispute between Plavsic and hardliners loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.

Plavsic dissolved parliament when hardliners tried to sabotage her attempts to expose large-scale corruption. Serb media, controlled by Karadzic loyalists, have accused Plavsic of provoking political turmoil which allowed NATO to strike at the war crimes suspects.
"We have many enemies who want to destroy the Serb republic and we have to be aware of it," Krajisnik told Serb television.
NATO officers previously had spoken of a possible violent backlash if suspects were arrested but there were no reprisals or serious threats against peacekeeping troops after the raid.
Krajisnik has appealed for calm and emphasised the need to maintain cooperation with the 31,000-strong NATO-led peace force.
The U.N. tribunal was scheduled to pronounce a sentence on Monday in the case of Dusan Tadic, a Bosnian Serb convicted of killing and torturing Moslems at detention camps around Prijedor.
Western diplomats say prosecuting war crimes is a crucial step in building post-war reconciliation and clearing the way for the scheduled withdrawal of NATO troops within a year.

NATO declined to discuss whether there would be more arrests but the raid in Prijedor and the use of sealed indictments raised expectations that more suspects would be seized in Bosnia's Serb and Moslem-Croat entities.
The shift in tactics also fed speculation that the two most prominent suspects on the published list of indictments -- Karadzic and his former army commander General Ratko Mladic -- might be next.
